analysis.one_liner: Abolishes the Treasury office that studies risks threatening the financial system.
analysis.headline: Sponsored by one senator with two cosponsors, the bill to eliminate the Office of Financial Research never received a committee vote and died when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would repeal the Office of Financial Research, a Treasury office created by the 2010 Dodd-Frank law that collects financial data and does analysis for the Financial Stability Oversight Council — the panel of regulators that watches for dangers that could crash the financial system, like the one that led to the 2008 crisis. Senator Ted Cruz introduced it in March 2021 with two Republican cosponsors. It never received a vote in the Senate Banking Committee and died when that Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: The largest banks and other big financial firms. The Office of Financial Research collects data from financial companies and performs the analysis regulators use to identify and monitor firms whose failure could destabilize the economy. Repealing the office would free those companies from that data collection and from the independent scrutiny it enables.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Large banks and Wall Street firms

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the entire section of the Dodd-Frank law that created the Office of Financial Research, eliminating the Treasury office that provides financial data and analysis to the Financial Stability Oversight Council.

Strips the Financial Stability Oversight Council's authority to act through the office and removes its role in monitoring systemically important firms, leaving large financial companies without the independent research arm that supports their heightened oversight.

analysis.who_pays: Ordinary taxpayers, savers, and workers. The office exists so regulators can spot building risks in the financial system before they become crises; without it, the burden of an unwatched financial failure — layoffs, lost savings, and potential taxpayer-funded bailouts like those after 2008 — falls on the public.

drawbacks.text: Eliminates the government's independent early-warning system for financial risk, weakening the oversight structure Congress built after the 2008 crisis to catch problems before they force rescues.

Repealing the office's full statutory subtitle removes not just the office but its data-collection and funding framework, leaving the Financial Stability Oversight Council's member agencies to gather and analyze system-wide risk data on their own.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits flow almost entirely to the largest financial firms, which would submit less data and face less independent scrutiny. The cost falls on everyone else: Congress created the office after 2008 precisely so regulators could see systemic risks building in time to act, and repealing it would leave the Financial Stability Oversight Council without its research arm. For households whose savings and jobs depend on avoiding another taxpayer-financed financial crisis, the cost clearly outweighs the benefit.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate Banking Committee never took the bill up, and it expired when that Congress ended in January 2023.

narrative.text: Senator Ted Cruz introduced the bill on March 2, 2021, to repeal the Office of Financial Research created by the Dodd-Frank law, with Senators Tom Cotton and Mike Braun as cosponsors.
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee on the day it was introduced.
The committee never scheduled a markup or vote, and no floor action ever occurred; the bill expired when the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The public and the financial regulators who keep the Office of Financial Research: because the bill died, the independent office that collects data on large financial firms and analyzes systemic risk for the Financial Stability Oversight Council remains in place. Large banks and financial firms, which the bill would have freed from that scrutiny, are worse off than they would have been under the bill.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Regulators and the public kept their watchdog

for.name: Sen. Ted Cruz
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to repeal the Office of Financial Research.

against.name: Senate Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee
against.role: Committee of jurisdiction (chaired by Sen. Sherrod Brown, D-OH)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral and never scheduled a markup or vote; the bill sat in committee until the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: Only three Republican senators were attached to the bill — the sponsor and two cosponsors out of 50 Senate Republicans — and no chamber ever voted on it, so the partisan shape of any potential vote was never tested.

industries.industry: Large banks and systemically important financial firms
industries.note: Repeal would end the Office of Financial Research's data collection from these firms and the independent analysis behind regulators' decisions to subject the biggest companies to heightened oversight. Less monitoring means a greater chance that a large firm's failure lands on taxpayers and the broader economy, as in 2008.

industries.industry: Systemically important insurers and other nonbank financial companies
industries.note: The Financial Stability Oversight Council can designate nonbank firms, including insurers, for stricter Federal Reserve supervision, and the office supplies data and analysis supporting that work. The bill strikes the council's ability to act through the office, weakening the pipeline that leads to nonbank designations.
